Source code and rules (GitHub) · 日本語

FPGA cores: verified against hardware or MAME?

Not an accuracy rating. The needle shows which reference a core's developers say, in its public source, they checked it against: the original hardware or MAME. It does not measure how accurate the core is. MAME is accurate for many boards, so a core at the MAME end can play correctly, and one at the hardware end can still have bugs. "Mostly hardware" is the top reading; a needle further right means more such statements, not a better core.

Was each MiSTer arcade core checked against the original arcade hardware, or against MAME? This page answers from what each core's own source says: its code comments, readme and shipped documentation. Statements pointing to MAME move the meter's white marker left; statements pointing to the original hardware move it right. Open a core's “▶ Statements” to see every statement, linked to its line at that commit; items that point at MAME link to the matching line in MAME (commit 78e14fa58b). Covered: every arcade core in update_all's three default databases, in six independent databases developers publish themselves, and in public repositories found by search, each read at the commit its distributed build came from.

Taken at face value. These are the developers' own statements, not independently checked. A core may be verified more, or less, than its comments say. Open source makes a false claim easy to expose, which is why developers' own words are a reasonable starting point. This method reads source code, so closed-source cores cannot be assessed this way and are shown separately; black-box testing against the original hardware or MAME would still be possible, but is far more work and is not done here.

Only public statements count. Comments, decap photos, probe measurements, board traces and other evidence posted on private sites (Patreon and other subscriber-only pages, closed Discord servers) are not counted, because they are not public statements: a reader cannot check them, and quoting them here would republish them. Work that has been done but not written into the public source does not move the meter.

How the needle is placed

Each comment (or readme sentence) is classified by the rules below. Within a module a rule adds its points × log2(1 + times it fired), so repetition counts for less than variety. A module's position is (hardware points + 1) / (all points + 2), from MAME at 0 to hardware at 100. A core's needle is the size-weighted average over modules that contain statements; the readme and the shipped documentation files each count like a quarter of the code. Modules with no statements are left out and reported as coverage. See RULES.md for the reasoning behind each rule.

StatementPointsSideIncludes
Cites hardware documentation that MAME's driver does not+0.5hardwareschematic sheet, part number, chip location, dumped PAL, decap — only when MAME's driver for the game does not already give it
Cites hardware references or measurements that MAME's driver also gives0neithernot counted: copying them from MAME would look the same
Says it was checked against the original PCB+2hardwareexplicitly the original board, PCB or arcade hardware
Reports a measurement taken on the original PCB+3hardwarestates a value; measurements of the MiSTer itself (e.g. SignalTap) do not count
Says it was checked on “real hardware”+1hardwaremay mean the MiSTer board itself rather than the original PCB, so it counts less
Ships hardware documentation files+2hardwareschematic sheets, schematic PDFs, PAL equations in the core's own folder
Notes where it differs from MAME+3hardwarea stated difference implies another reference
Cites MAME source−0.5MAMEa MAME file, function or line
Says it matches, follows or was checked against MAME−2MAMEincludes “ground truth: MAME”
Says it was translated, ported or taken from MAME−3MAME
Keeps a MAME approximation−1MAMEwhere MAME itself notes a guess or stand-in
Shares text with the MAME driver without saying so−1MAMEa 6-word run in a comment

Not counted: ROM file names (MiSTer uses MAME's ROM sets by design) and memory addresses (a correct core must share them with any correct emulator). Quoted comments remain under their authors' licenses; this analysis is published under CC BY 4.0.
